subtype: Approach: trying to memorise everything in the encyclopedia [Pitfall]
passage: Anders had three weeks before the school quiz in Copenhagen and one big idea: read the whole encyclopedia. He carried the heavy blue volume to bed every night and started at page one. By day four he had reached the letter B, and the facts all swam together: bats, Bangkok, barometers. His sister Clara asked him, "What is the capital of Peru?" He frowned. "It's in there somewhere." Anders realised he could not tell which facts were likely to come up, or which topics he already knew. His eyes were tired, and the book felt as heavy as a brick. He closed it with a groan.

qa.q: How many days had Anders been reading when he reached the letter B?
qa.a: Anders had been reading for four days.

qa.q: What did Anders feel when he could not answer Clara's question about Peru?
qa.a: Anders felt tired, confused and a little discouraged, since he could not find the fact he had read among all the others. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anders use, and why?
qa.a: Anders could find out the quiz topics and format first, then practise mock rounds with a partner. That shows which facts matter and where he is weak.

qa.q: How might Clara see Anders's plan?
qa.a: Clara asked a simple question and saw her brother frown, so Clara probably sees that the plan is not working and may want to help him choose a better way.

grounding: A child decides to learn all the facts in a thick book but soon gets tired and confused, not knowing which facts matter or where he is weak.

subtype: Approach: trying to memorise everything in the encyclopedia [Pitfall]
passage: Three weeks before the inter-school quiz, Vaibhav walked into the school library and asked Jahnavi ma'am for the thickest encyclopaedia. "I'm going to learn all of it." She raised an eyebrow but handed it over. Every free period he sat at the corner table and read: A for aardvark, abacus, Abu Dhabi. By the fourth day he was on B and could not remember what an abacus was. By the second week his eyes hurt, he had forgotten most of A, and he still didn't know whether the quiz even had animal questions. On Friday he closed the book with a thump and put his head on it. Jahnavi ma'am came over quietly. "Shall we find out what the quiz actually asks?"

qa.q: Where did Vaibhav sit to read during free periods?
qa.a: He sat at the corner table in the library.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when he closed the book with a thump?
qa.a: He felt tired, frustrated and defeated, since weeks of reading had left him confused.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Vaibhav better, and why?
qa.a: Finding out the quiz topics first and testing himself to find weak areas, because then he can study what matters.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav's plan look to Jahnavi ma'am?
qa.a: Jahnavi ma'am doubts it from the start, and when he gives up she gently offers a better way.

grounding: It shows a child trying to learn a whole encyclopaedia, becoming tired and confused, and not knowing which facts matter or where he is weak.

subtype: Approach: trying to memorise everything in the encyclopedia [Pitfall]
passage: My younger brother Chetan decided in June that he would win the district quiz by memorising the big red general knowledge book. All of it. Nine hundred pages. I watched him from the other bed. Every night he read under the table lamp, lips moving. The first week he was excited and kept telling me facts at breakfast. The second week he stopped telling me facts. The third week he fell asleep on page two hundred with the light on. When our cousin Ramesh tested him with an old quiz sheet, Chetan got seven out of thirty. He stared at the sheet. "I read all of this," he said. "Where did it go?" I don't know what he felt exactly. He didn't open the book the next night.

qa.q: How many pages did the red general knowledge book have?
What might Chetan be feeling when he asks where it all went?
qa.a: He is probably confused and discouraged, maybe hurt, after so much reading led to seven out of thirty.

qa.q: What else could Chetan try instead of reading the whole book?
qa.a: He could study old quiz sheets first to see what gets asked and where he is weak, then read only those parts.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh sees the gap between the reading and the score, and the test he gives shows Chetan the plan is not working.

grounding: It shows a child trying to memorise a whole thick book, getting tired and confused, and not knowing which facts matter.
